meta.name: When to Spay or Neuter a Dog: The Best Age by Size, Breed and Sex
meta.title_tag: When to Spay or Neuter a Dog: Best Age by Size
meta.excerpt: Six months is no longer the automatic answer. Here's what AAHA, the AVMA, WSAVA and 2026 UK guidance say about when to spay or neuter a dog by size and breed, what the UC Davis data show, the real trade-offs, and what to ask your vet.
meta.meta_description: When to spay or neuter a dog by size and breed: what AAHA, WSAVA and 2026 BVA guidance say, the UC Davis data, benefits, risks and vet questions.
meta.author: Kailun Zhang

hero.alt: Young Golden Retriever sitting calmly in a bright veterinary exam room

body_html:
Quick Answer: There's no single right age. AAHA suggests about 5–6 months for dogs expected to weigh under 45 lb as adults, and waiting until growth stops (about 9–15 months) for larger males, with larger females decided case by case. Newer UK guidance favors 12–24 months for most dogs (BVA/BSAVA 2026), and UC Davis data suggest 1–2 years for some large breeds. Make the call with your vet. Questions to ask your vet ↓

Why Six Months Stopped Being Automatic

Spaying or neutering in the first year became routine in the US and much of Europe, increasingly by 6 months (Hart et al., 2020). UC Davis researchers then sorted hospital records by breed, sex and age at surgery. In Golden Retrievers, Labradors and German Shepherds, neutering before a year was linked to two to four times the intact rate of hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia or cruciate ligament tears. Yet across 35 breeds, most showed no added joint or cancer risk at any age (Hart et al., 2020).

What the Major Guidelines Say

All call for individual decisions, but defaults differ:

GuidelineWhat it recommends
AAHA 2019 (US)Under 45 lb adult weight: males at 6 months, females before the first heat (5–6 months). 45 lb and up: males when growth stops (about 9–15 months), females at 5–15 months, case by case.
AVMA (US)No one-size-fits-all age; decide with your vet.
WSAVA 2024 (global)Doesn't recommend spaying or neutering before puberty in any breed (Romagnoli, 2025).
BVA/BSAVA 2026 (UK)Most dogs at 12–24 months. Females at 12–23 months by breed; males case by case, and not before physical maturity without a compelling reason.
ASV 2022 (shelters)Sterilize before adoption or ensure it happens after; safe in healthy animals from 6 weeks.

The biggest split is over small females: AAHA favors spaying before the first heat to cut mammary tumor risk, while WSAVA and the BVA lean later. AAHA also calls the evidence on timing and orthopedic disease too thin for firm conclusions.

Best Age to Spay or Neuter by Size

AAHA's cutoff is 45 lb; UC Davis uses 20 kg (about 44 lb). Treat these as starting points:

Expected adult weightStarting pointWhy
Under 20 kg (about 44 lb)About 6 months (AAHA)No added joint risk at any neutering age in mixed breeds (Hart et al., 2020)
20–40 kg (about 44–88 lb)At least 12 months (Hart et al., 2020); AAHA: males at 9–15 monthsNeutering before 1 year commonly tripled joint disorders in mixed breeds (Hart et al., 2020)
Over 40 kg (about 88 lb)Males about 2 years; females about 1 year (Hart et al., 2020)Neutering males before 6 months tripled joint disorders, 28% vs 9% intact (Hart et al., 2020)

Removing the ovaries or testes before growth ends delays growth-plate closure (Salmeri et al., 1991), which the WSAVA's lead author links to orthopedic disease in larger and especially giant breeds (Romagnoli, 2025). In the prospective Golden Retriever Lifetime Study, dogs neutered at 6 months or younger had about four times the risk of orthopedic injury (Simpson et al., 2019).

Breed Matters: What the UC Davis Data Show

Breed can override size. Figures are the share of dogs with at least one joint disorder or one of four cancers in UC Davis records (Hart et al., 2020; Hart et al., 2024):

BreedWhat the records showedSuggested timing
Labrador RetrieverJoint disorders 6% intact; 13% in males neutered before 6 months; 11–12% in females spayed before 1 yearMales after 6 months; females after 1 year
Golden RetrieverJoint disorders 5% in intact males, 25% if neutered before 6 months; cancers 5% in intact females, 11–17% if spayed at any ageMales after 1 year; females intact, or spayed at 1 year with cancer monitoring
German Shepherd DogJoint disorders 6% in intact males, 18–19% if neutered before 1 year; up to 9% incontinence in females spayed by 1 yearBoth sexes after 2 years
Rottweiler43% of females spayed before 6 months had a joint disorder (16% intact); 12% of intact females had pyometraMales after 1 year; females after 6 months
Bernese Mountain DogJoint disorders 23–24% in males neutered before 2 years (4% intact)Males well after 2 years
Mastiff (2024)Males neutered before 1 year: cancers 28% (7% intact), joint disorders 21% (6%)Males from 24 months; females from 12 months
Siberian Husky (2024)No significant effectsMales from 6 months; females from 12 months, as a precaution
Great DaneNo joint or cancer increaseOwner's choice; authors suggest well past 1 year

Separately, Rottweilers neutered before a year had about a one in four lifetime risk of bone cancer, three to four times the intact rate (Cooley et al., 2002).

The limits: these are one teaching hospital's records, reviewed after the fact. They show associations, not proof of cause, and mammary cancer was likely undercounted because records often ended too early (Hart et al., 2020).

Benefits and Risks at a Glance

Benefits

  • No accidental litters (Merck).
  • No pyometra. About 1 in 4 intact females in Swedish insurance data had this uterine infection by age 10, up to 54% in some breeds (Egenvall et al., 2001). It's a potentially life-threatening emergency (Cornell).
  • No testicular cancer, and less benign prostate enlargement (AVMA).
  • Longer average life. In US teaching-hospital records, sterilized dogs died at 9.4 years on average versus 7.9 for intact dogs, though more often of cancer (Hoffman et al., 2013): an association, not proof.

Risks

  • Joint disorders in some larger breeds after early surgery; our arthritis home-setup guide covers long-term joint care.
  • Some cancers. AAHA lists higher risk of osteosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma, mast cell tumors, and prostate, bladder and anal gland cancers, varying by breed. Overall osteosarcoma incidence is about 0.2%.
  • Urinary incontinence, more common in spayed females (AAHA); 25% of Dobermans spayed before 6 months had it in UC Davis data (Hart et al., 2020).
  • Weight gain at any neutering age in Golden Retrievers (Simpson et al., 2019), most likely in the two years after surgery (AAHA). Diet and exercise manage it (AVMA).
  • Surgery and anesthesia, typically low risk (AVMA).

Should You Spay Before or After the First Heat?

The classic case for early spaying is mammary cancer: AAHA cites figures of 8% after one heat and 26% after two, from a 1969 study that measured risk relative to intact dogs, not lifetime rates (Guirguis & Beggs, 2025). The AVMA sees no known benefit in waiting for a first heat.

That evidence is weaker than it sounds. A 2012 systematic review judged it weak, with 9 of 13 studies at high risk of bias (Beauvais et al., 2012). A 2025 review was split: 7 of 13 studies found early spaying protective and 6 found no evidence it was (Guirguis & Beggs, 2025), and a 2024 review concluded that robust evidence on timing relative to puberty doesn't yet exist (Moxon et al., 2024).

First heats range from 4 to 24 months by breed (AAHA). For small females, spaying before the first heat remains mainstream US advice. For large females, AAHA weighs mammary tumors and unwanted litters against joint disease, some cancers and incontinence, case by case.

Will Spaying or Neutering Change Behavior?

It often helps sex-driven habits: in 57 males neutered after age 2, marking, mounting and roaming improved by at least half in 60% or more (Neilson et al., 1997). For fear and aggression, don't count on it:

  • Fewer than 35% improved by half or more for aggression (Neilson et al., 1997).
  • In more than 13,000 dogs, neutering showed no link with aggression toward family or other dogs; those neutered at 7–12 months were 26% more likely to be aggressive toward strangers (Farhoody et al., 2018).
  • In 6,235 castrated males, longer hormone exposure before surgery went with fewer reports of several fear- and aggression-related behaviors (McGreevy et al., 2018). These are survey associations.

AAHA adds that behavior changes during social maturity, about 12 to 36 months, aren't linked to hormones or sexual maturity (AAHA 2015). For a limit-testing adolescent, our guides to the dog teenage phase and leash reactive dogs will help more than surgery.

Hormone-Sparing Options: Ovary-Sparing Spay and Vasectomy

An ovary-sparing spay (removing the uterus but keeping the ovaries) and a vasectomy prevent pregnancy but keep hormones, so sex-driven behaviors continue (AVMA). After an ovary-sparing spay, females still cycle but have no bloody discharge or pyometra risk (Hart et al., 2024 editorial), provided the whole uterus comes out; leftover uterine tissue in a cycling dog can still become infected (Cornell). These dogs still need mammary or prostate checks, and the procedures appear as safe as standard surgery (Romagnoli, 2025). Not every clinic offers them.

Living With an Intact Dog Until Then

  • Heat cycles. Most females cycle about twice a year. The bleeding phase and the fertile phase each average about 9 days, and she attracts males throughout (Merck). Keep her leashed or supervised, and skip dog parks and daycare.
  • Pyometra watch. It often appears one to two months after a heat. Discharge, lethargy, poor appetite, vomiting or increased thirst means an urgent vet visit (Cornell).
  • Intact males. AAHA flags the hazards of roaming. Check fences and build a reliable recall.
  • Accidental mating. Call your vet promptly to discuss options (Merck).

Adopting? Shelter Rules and Large-Breed Puppies

Shelters prioritize population control. Some places, including California, require pre-adoption sterilization (ASV; Hart et al., 2020). AAHA accepts that factors like future vet access can shape timing. Adopting a large-breed puppy? Ask whether a later, post-adoption surgery date is possible, and get it in writing.

Questions to Ask Your Vet

  1. What adult weight do you expect, and when will my dog stop growing?
  2. Does my dog's breed or mix have timing-related risks?
  3. For a female: when is her first heat likely, and how do you weigh mammary tumors and pyometra against joints?
  4. For a male: is there a reason to neuter now? And do you offer vasectomy or ovary-sparing spay?
  5. Could surgery be combined with another procedure (AAHA), such as the gastropexy in our Great Dane puppy checklist?

Written by Kailun Zhang, who is not a veterinarian. This guide summarizes the veterinary sources listed below and isn't a substitute for advice from your vet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best age to spay or neuter a dog?

It depends on size, breed and sex. AAHA suggests about 5–6 months for dogs under 45 lb as adults and later for larger dogs, especially males. UK guidance favors 12–24 months for most dogs (BVA/BSAVA 2026).

When should I spay a large breed dog?

AAHA gives females expected to reach 45 lb or more a 5–15 month window. UC Davis data suggest at least 1 year for many large breeds and 2 years for German Shepherds (Hart et al., 2020).

Should I let my dog have one heat before spaying?

Not for her health: the AVMA says there's no known benefit to waiting until after a first heat. In some breeds, though, delaying a spay to protect the joints means it may fall after a first heat (AAHA).

Is 6 months too early to neuter a dog?

For most small dogs, no: UC Davis found no added joint risk in small breeds or mixed breeds under 20 kg (Hart et al., 2020). For some large breeds it may be; Golden Retrievers neutered at 6 months or younger had about four times the risk of orthopedic injury (Simpson et al., 2019).

Will neutering calm my dog down?

It often reduces marking, mounting and roaming (Neilson et al., 1997), but it isn't a fix for energy, fear or aggression. In more than 13,000 dogs, neutering showed no link with aggression toward family or other dogs (Farhoody et al., 2018).

Is it too late to spay or neuter an older dog?

Usually not. Castration after age 2 still reduced marking, mounting and roaming (Neilson et al., 1997), and spaying prevents pyometra, which is most common in middle-aged and older intact females (Cornell).
